disclaimer: Estimated by Ayuvo from your own data using published formulas. It is not a medical measurement or diagnosis; talk to your doctor about anything that concerns you.

metrics.about: Your lowest steady heart rate while asleep, estimated from minute-by-minute heart rate when your device does not provide a resting heart rate.
metrics.citation: Nocturnal minimum heart rate as a resting-heart-rate estimate, as used by consumer wearables; adult resting range 60-100 bpm per American Heart Association, lower in trained people.
metrics.method: Lowest average of 5 consecutive minutes inside last night's main sleep. Needs at least 3 hours of sleep with heart rate on at least 70% of those minutes.
metrics.title: Resting Heart Rate (estimated)

metrics.about: Average heart rate across last night's main sleep.
metrics.citation: Descriptive statistic of nocturnal heart rate.
metrics.method: Mean of every heart-rate minute inside the main sleep window.
metrics.title: Sleeping Heart Rate

metrics.about: The single lowest heart-rate reading during last night's sleep.
metrics.citation: Descriptive statistic of nocturnal heart rate.
metrics.method: Minimum heart-rate minute inside the main sleep window.
metrics.title: Lowest Heart Rate at Night

metrics.about: How much lower your heart rate is asleep than awake. A dip of 10% or more is the usual healthy pattern.
metrics.citation: Nocturnal heart-rate dipping (≥10%) by analogy with blood-pressure dipping; Ben-Dov IZ et al., Hypertension 2007; Eguchi K et al., Am J Hypertens 2009.
metrics.method: 1 − (sleeping average ÷ awake average over the 14 hours after waking) × 100. Needs at least 4 hours of awake heart rate.
metrics.title: Night-time Heart Rate Dip

metrics.about: Your heart rate while sitting still during the day (09:00-21:00), when you took no steps for at least 10 minutes.
metrics.citation: Resting-while-awake heart rate; adult resting range 60-100 bpm (American Heart Association).
metrics.method: Mean of daytime heart-rate minutes where the current and previous 10 minutes had no steps. Needs 30 such minutes.
metrics.title: Sedentary Daytime Heart Rate

metrics.about: Average, lowest and highest heart rate while awake today.
metrics.citation: Descriptive statistic.
metrics.method: Mean, minimum and maximum of heart-rate minutes outside the main sleep window. Needs 60 minutes.
metrics.title: Daytime Heart Rate

metrics.about: Highest heart rate held for at least 2 minutes today.
metrics.citation: Artefact rejection by short rolling average.
metrics.method: Maximum of 2-minute rolling averages, which ignores single-reading spikes.
metrics.title: Highest Heart Rate

metrics.about: Your estimated maximum heart rate, used to set heart-rate zones.
metrics.citation: Tanaka H, Monahan KD, Seals DR. Age-predicted maximal heart rate revisited. J Am Coll Cardiol 2001;37:153-156.
metrics.method: Tanaka formula 208 − 0.7 × age, raised to the highest 2-minute heart rate seen in the last 180 days when that is higher.
metrics.title: Maximum Heart Rate

metrics.about: The gap between your maximum and resting heart rate. A larger reserve usually means better fitness.
metrics.citation: American College of Sports Medicine. ACSM's Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription, 11th ed. (2021), intensity classification by % heart-rate reserve (Karvonen) and % HRmax.
metrics.method: Maximum heart rate − resting heart rate (Karvonen).
metrics.title: Heart Rate Reserve

metrics.about: Minutes your heart rate was in the moderate or vigorous range, with vigorous minutes counted twice. WHO recommends 150-300 a week.
metrics.citation: American College of Sports Medicine. ACSM's Guidelines for Exercise Testing and Prescription, 11th ed. (2021), intensity classification by % heart-rate reserve (Karvonen) and % HRmax. World Health Organization. WHO guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour (2020): 150-300 min/week moderate or 75-150 min/week vigorous; vigorous minutes count double.
metrics.method: Each heart-rate minute is classed by % heart-rate reserve (moderate 40-59%, vigorous 60-89%, near-maximal ≥90%). Without a resting heart rate % of maximum is used (moderate 64-76%, vigorous 77-95%, near-maximal ≥96%). Moderate + 2 × (vigorous + near-maximal).
metrics.title: Cardio Minutes

metrics.about: A load score that weighs time by how hard your heart worked. Harder minutes count exponentially more.
metrics.citation: Banister EW. Modeling elite athletic performance. In: MacDougall JD, Wenger HA, Green HJ, eds. Physiological Testing of the High-Performance Athlete. 2nd ed. Human Kinetics; 1991:403-424. Morton RH et al., J Appl Physiol 1990;69(3):1171-1177.
metrics.method: Banister TRIMP over minutes at ≥30% heart-rate reserve: Σ minutes × HRr × a × e^(k × HRr), with a = 0.64, k = 1.92 for men and a = 0.86, k = 1.67 for women (the midpoint for other).
metrics.title: Training Impulse (TRIMP)

metrics.about: An estimate of your VO₂max from your maximum and resting heart rate. It is a rough guide; an outdoor GPS workout gives a better estimate.
metrics.citation: Uth N, Sørensen H, Overgaard K, Pedersen PK. Estimation of VO2max from the ratio between HRmax and HRrest. Eur J Appl Physiol 2004;91:111-115.
metrics.method: Uth-Sørensen: 15.3 × maximum heart rate ÷ resting heart rate. Low confidence when the maximum comes from the age formula.
metrics.title: Cardio Fitness (estimated)

metrics.about: How far today's resting heart rate is from your 30-day average. Two days in a row 5 bpm or more above usual can mean strain, poor sleep or getting ill.
metrics.citation: Resting-heart-rate elevation as a strain and illness signal: Radin JM et al., Lancet Digital Health 2020; Buchheit M, Front Physiol 2014.
metrics.method: Today − mean of the previous 30 days (needs 14 days). Flag when today and yesterday are both at least 5 bpm above.
metrics.title: Resting Heart Rate vs Usual

metrics.about: How many minutes today your wearable recorded heart rate. A day with 10 hours or more is counted as a valid day.
metrics.citation: Valid-day rule of ≥10 h wear from accelerometry research: Troiano RP et al., Med Sci Sports Exerc 2008.
metrics.method: Count of minutes with a heart-rate reading in the local day.
metrics.title: Wear Time

metrics.about: Your average heart rate while walking. It usually falls as fitness improves.
metrics.citation: Walking heart rate average as a fitness marker (Apple Heart and Movement Study methodology).
metrics.method: Mean heart rate in minutes with 60-130 steps, in runs of 3 or more such minutes (faster minutes count as running). Needs 10 minutes.
metrics.title: Walking Heart Rate

metrics.about: Share of your time in bed spent asleep. 85% or more is considered good.
metrics.citation: Ohayon M et al. National Sleep Foundation's sleep quality recommendations. Sleep Health 2017;3:6-19 (efficiency ≥85%).
metrics.method: Time asleep ÷ time in bed × 100.
metrics.title: Sleep Efficiency

metrics.about: How long it took to fall asleep after getting into bed. Up to 30 minutes is typical.
metrics.citation: Ohayon M et al., Sleep Health 2017 (latency ≤30 min).
metrics.method: First asleep stage − start of time in bed. Needs an In Bed record.
metrics.title: Time to Fall Asleep

metrics.about: Share of sleep spent in deep sleep. Adults usually spend about 13-23%.
metrics.citation: Ohayon MM et al. Meta-analysis of quantitative sleep parameters. Sleep 2004;27:1255-1273.
metrics.method: Deep minutes ÷ time asleep × 100. Only nights with sleep stages.
metrics.title: Deep Sleep

metrics.about: Share of sleep spent in REM. Adults usually spend about 20-25%.
metrics.citation: Ohayon MM et al., Sleep 2004.
metrics.method: REM minutes ÷ time asleep × 100. Only nights with sleep stages.
metrics.title: REM Sleep

metrics.about: Times you were awake for 5 minutes or more after first falling asleep.
metrics.citation: Wake after sleep onset (WASO), Ohayon M et al., Sleep Health 2017.
metrics.method: Gaps of ≥5 minutes between asleep stages, from first sleep to final waking. Minutes awake are shown as wake after sleep onset.
metrics.title: Wake-ups

metrics.about: When your night started.
metrics.citation: Descriptive.
metrics.method: Start of the first sleep record, as a clock time.
metrics.title: Bedtime

metrics.about: When you finally woke up.
metrics.citation: Descriptive.
metrics.method: End of the last asleep stage, as a clock time.
metrics.title: Wake Time

metrics.about: Halfway between falling asleep and waking. It tracks your body-clock timing.
metrics.citation: Roenneberg T et al. Life between clocks. J Biol Rhythms 2003.
metrics.method: Sleep onset + half the time to final waking.
metrics.title: Sleep Midpoint

metrics.about: Minutes from falling asleep to the first deep sleep.
metrics.citation: Descriptive (sleep architecture).
metrics.method: First deep stage − sleep onset.
metrics.title: Time to First Deep Sleep

metrics.about: Minutes from falling asleep to the first REM sleep. Typically 70-120 minutes.
metrics.citation: Carskadon MA, Dement WC. Normal human sleep: an overview. Principles and Practice of Sleep Medicine.
metrics.method: First REM stage − sleep onset.
metrics.title: Time to First REM

metrics.about: How much your bedtime varies across the last 14 nights. Under 30-60 minutes is regular.
metrics.citation: Sleep timing regularity; Phillips AJK et al., Sci Rep 2017.
metrics.method: Sample standard deviation of bedtime (and wake time) over the last 14 nights. Needs 5 nights.
metrics.title: Bedtime Variability

metrics.about: The chance you are in the same state (asleep or awake) at the same time on consecutive days, scaled to 100. Higher is more regular.
metrics.citation: Phillips AJK et al. Irregular sleep/wake patterns are associated with poorer academic performance and delayed circadian and sleep/wake timing. Sci Rep 2017;7:3216.
metrics.method: Minute-by-minute comparison of each noon-to-noon day with the next over the last 14 days: 200 × agreement − 100. Needs 5 day pairs.
metrics.title: Sleep Regularity Index

metrics.about: How much later you sleep on weekends than on weekdays. Under 1 hour is best.
metrics.citation: Wittmann M, Dinich J, Merrow M, Roenneberg T. Social jetlag. Chronobiol Int 2006;23:497-509.
metrics.method: |Mean sleep midpoint on free nights (waking Saturday or Sunday) − on work nights|. Needs 2 free and 3 work nights in 14 days.
metrics.title: Social Jet Lag

metrics.about: Your natural body-clock timing: the midpoint of sleep on free days, corrected for catching up on sleep.
metrics.citation: Roenneberg T et al. Epidemiology of the human circadian clock. Sleep Med Rev 2007;11:429-438.
metrics.method: MSFsc = MSF − (SDf − SDweek) ÷ 2 when free-day sleep is longer than weekday sleep, where SDweek = (5 × SDw + 2 × SDf) ÷ 7.
metrics.title: Chronotype (MSFsc)

metrics.about: Sleep you missed against your nightly need over the last 14 nights. Adults need at least 7 hours.
metrics.citation: Watson NF et al. Recommended amount of sleep for a healthy adult (AASM/SRS). Sleep 2015;38:843-844.
metrics.method: Σ max(0, need − time asleep) over recorded nights in the last 14 days. Need defaults to 8 hours.
metrics.title: Sleep Debt

metrics.about: Minutes you walked at 100 steps a minute or faster, which counts as moderate activity.
metrics.citation: Tudor-Locke C et al. Walking cadence (steps/min) and intensity in 21-40 year olds: CADENCE-adults. Int J Behav Nutr Phys Act 2019; Tudor-Locke C et al., Br J Sports Med 2018.
metrics.method: Minutes with ≥100 steps from your wearable's minute data.
metrics.title: Brisk Walking Minutes

metrics.about: The average of your 30 fastest minutes of stepping today.
metrics.citation: Tudor-Locke C et al. Peak stepping cadence in free-living adults. J Phys Act Health 2011.
metrics.method: Mean of the 30 highest minute step counts in the day.
metrics.title: Peak 30-min Cadence

metrics.about: Hours between 07:00 and 22:00 with at least 250 steps. Breaking up sitting every hour is recommended.
metrics.citation: WHO 2020 guideline: limit sedentary time and replace it with activity of any intensity.
metrics.method: Count of hours 07:00-21:59 whose de-duplicated steps are ≥250.
metrics.title: Active Hours

metrics.about: Your longest run of minutes without a step between 07:00 and 22:00 while wearing your device.
metrics.citation: WHO 2020 guideline on sedentary behaviour.
metrics.method: Longest run of worn minutes (heart rate present) with no steps, 07:00-21:59.
metrics.title: Longest Sitting Spell

metrics.about: Your daily steps placed in the Tudor-Locke bands: sedentary <5,000, low active 5,000-7,499, somewhat active 7,500-9,999, active 10,000-12,499, highly active ≥12,500.
metrics.citation: Tudor-Locke C et al. How many steps/day are enough? for adults. Int J Behav Nutr Phys Act 2011;8:79.
metrics.method: Band of the day's de-duplicated step total.
metrics.title: Activity Level

metrics.about: Steps your wearable counted while your phone counted almost none, for example when the phone stayed at home.
metrics.citation: Data-quality rule.
metrics.method: Flagged when the wearable counts ≥1,000 steps and the phone less than 10% of that.
metrics.title: Phone-free Steps

metrics.about: Consecutive days you reached your step goal.
metrics.citation: Descriptive.
metrics.method: Days in a row meeting the goal, counting today once it is met.
metrics.title: Step Goal Streak

metrics.about: Average step length from your phone's distance and steps, compared with the typical length for your height.
metrics.citation: Hatano Y. Use of the pedometer for promoting daily walking exercise. ICHPER 1993.
metrics.method: Distance ÷ steps from the same source (needs 1,000 steps). Typical = 0.415 × height for men and 0.413 × height for women.
metrics.title: Stride Length

metrics.about: All the energy your body used today: resting, activity and digesting food.
metrics.citation: Westerterp KR. Diet induced thermogenesis. Nutr Metab 2004;1:5.
metrics.method: (Resting + active energy) ÷ 0.9, adding about 10% for digestion. Needs a full day of resting energy (at least 70% of your predicted BMR).
metrics.title: Total Energy Burned

metrics.about: Energy used at rest per day from your device, next to the Mifflin-St Jeor prediction.
metrics.citation: Mifflin MD et al. A new predictive equation for resting energy expenditure. Am J Clin Nutr 1990;51:241-247.
metrics.method: Daily resting energy; prediction 10 × kg + 6.25 × cm − 5 × age + 5 (men) or − 161 (women).
metrics.title: Resting Metabolic Rate

metrics.about: Total energy burned ÷ resting energy. 1.40-1.69 is sedentary to lightly active, 1.70-1.99 active, 2.00-2.40 vigorously active.
metrics.citation: FAO/WHO/UNU. Human energy requirements. Food and Nutrition Technical Report Series 1, 2004.
metrics.method: TDEE ÷ resting energy.
metrics.title: Physical Activity Level

metrics.about: Your typical walking speed over the last 7 days. Below 0.8 m/s is linked with higher health risk in older adults.
metrics.citation: Studenski S et al. Gait speed and survival in older adults. JAMA 2011;305:50-58.
metrics.method: Median of walking-speed readings in the last 7 days.
metrics.title: Walking Speed (weekly)

metrics.about: Share of each step with both feet on the ground. Typical values are 20-40%; higher can mean less balance.
metrics.citation: Apple Inc. Measuring Walking Quality Through iPhone Mobility Metrics (2022).
metrics.method: Median of double-support readings in the last 7 days.
metrics.title: Double Support Time (weekly)

metrics.about: Walking readings in the last 7 days where one step was more than 10% different from the other.
metrics.citation: Apple Inc. Measuring Walking Quality Through iPhone Mobility Metrics (2022).
metrics.method: Count of asymmetry readings >10% (readings of 100% are treated as sensor errors). Flagged at 3 or more.
metrics.title: Uneven Walking Readings

metrics.about: How much of the weekly safe-listening allowance you used, where 100% a week is 80 dB for 40 hours.
metrics.citation: WHO-ITU H.870 Guidelines for safe listening devices/systems (2019).
metrics.method: Σ hours × 2^((dB − 80) ÷ 3) ÷ 40 × 100 (3 dB exchange rate).
metrics.title: Headphone Sound Dose

metrics.about: Your weight with day-to-day water swings smoothed out.
metrics.citation: Walker J. The Hacker's Diet (exponentially smoothed moving average, α = 0.1).
metrics.method: Exponentially smoothed average: trend += 0.1 × (weigh-in − trend) on each day with a weigh-in.
metrics.title: Weight Trend

metrics.about: How fast your smoothed weight is changing per week.
metrics.citation: Derived from the smoothed trend.
metrics.method: (Trend today − trend 14 days ago) ÷ 2. Needs 4 weigh-ins in 14 days.
metrics.title: Weekly Weight Change

metrics.about: Body mass index from your smoothed weight and height.
metrics.citation: WHO Expert Consultation. Appropriate body-mass index for Asian populations. Lancet 2004;363:157-163.
metrics.method: Trend weight ÷ height². WHO categories, or the Asian cut-offs (overweight ≥23, obese ≥27.5) if chosen in Settings.
metrics.title: BMI

metrics.about: The weight range with a healthy BMI for your height.
metrics.citation: WHO BMI classification.
metrics.method: 18.5 × height² to 24.9 × height² (22.9 with Asian cut-offs).
metrics.title: Healthy Weight Range

metrics.about: How many weeks until you reach your goal weight at your current rate.
metrics.citation: Derived from the smoothed trend.
metrics.method: (Goal − trend) ÷ weekly rate, when moving towards the goal at ≥0.05 kg a week.
metrics.title: Weeks to Goal Weight

metrics.about: Protein you logged per kilogram of body weight. 1.4-2.0 g/kg a day supports strength training.
metrics.citation: International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand: protein and exercise (Jäger R et al. 2017): 1.4-2.0 g/kg/day, about 0.25 g/kg per meal.
metrics.method: Logged protein ÷ latest weight.
metrics.title: Protein per kg

metrics.about: Share of your energy from protein, carbohydrate and fat, from the grams you logged.
metrics.citation: Atwater factors 4/4/9 kcal/g; WHO: saturated fat below 10% of energy; Dietary Guidelines for Americans: fiber 14 g per 1,000 kcal; WHO sodium/potassium molar ratio below 1.
metrics.method: 4 kcal/g protein and carbohydrate, 9 kcal/g fat; each share of their total.
metrics.title: Macro Split

metrics.about: Share of your energy from saturated fat. WHO recommends below 10%.
metrics.citation: Atwater factors 4/4/9 kcal/g; WHO: saturated fat below 10% of energy; Dietary Guidelines for Americans: fiber 14 g per 1,000 kcal; WHO sodium/potassium molar ratio below 1.
metrics.method: 9 × saturated fat g ÷ energy from macros × 100.
metrics.title: Saturated Fat

metrics.about: Fibre per 1,000 kcal you ate. About 14 g per 1,000 kcal is recommended.
metrics.citation: Atwater factors 4/4/9 kcal/g; WHO: saturated fat below 10% of energy; Dietary Guidelines for Americans: fiber 14 g per 1,000 kcal; WHO sodium/potassium molar ratio below 1.
metrics.method: Fibre g × 1,000 ÷ logged kcal.
metrics.title: Fibre per 1,000 kcal

metrics.about: Molar ratio of sodium to potassium. WHO suggests keeping it below 1. Salt added while cooking is often not in food estimates.
metrics.citation: Atwater factors 4/4/9 kcal/g; WHO: saturated fat below 10% of energy; Dietary Guidelines for Americans: fiber 14 g per 1,000 kcal; WHO sodium/potassium molar ratio below 1.
metrics.method: (sodium mg ÷ 22.99) ÷ (potassium mg ÷ 39.10).
metrics.title: Sodium to Potassium

metrics.about: Time from your first to your last logged food, using the time you ate it.
metrics.citation: Descriptive; uses each item's eaten-at time, not when it was logged.
metrics.method: Last eaten time − first eaten time.
metrics.title: Eating Window

metrics.about: Time between your last food and going to bed.
metrics.citation: Descriptive; uses the eaten-at time and the night's first sleep record.
metrics.method: Bedtime − last eaten time.
metrics.title: Last Meal to Bedtime

metrics.about: Times you had tea or coffee within an hour of an iron-rich food, which can reduce how much iron you absorb.
metrics.citation: Tea and coffee polyphenols inhibit non-heme iron absorption (Hurrell RF et al. Br J Nutr 1999).
metrics.method: Count of tea/coffee items within 60 minutes of an item with ≥3 mg iron.
metrics.title: Tea or Coffee with Iron-rich Food

metrics.about: Calories you logged minus the energy you burned today.
metrics.citation: Adaptive energy expenditure from intake and weight trend, about 7,700 kcal per kg of body-mass change (Hall KD, Int J Obes 2008 discusses its limits).
metrics.method: Logged kcal − total energy burned.
metrics.title: Energy Balance

metrics.about: What your body likely burns per day, worked out from what you ate and how your weight trend changed over 4 weeks.
metrics.citation: Adaptive energy expenditure from intake and weight trend, about 7,700 kcal per kg of body-mass change (Hall KD, Int J Obes 2008 discusses its limits).
metrics.method: Mean logged kcal − (trend change × 7,700 kcal/kg) ÷ 28 days. Needs 14 logged days and 6 weigh-ins.
metrics.title: Adaptive Energy Estimate
